nodes.label: Wuyts et al. (2002) described a boy with multiple exostoses, hypertrichosis, mental retardation, epilepsy, and brain abnormalities.

In a boy with multiple exostoses, hypertrichosis, mental retardation, and epilepsy, Wuyts et al. (2002) identified a de novo submicroscopic interstitial deletion of chromosome 8q24. On molecular analysis, the deletion overlapped the Langer-Giedion syndrome region and included the EXT1 gene and additional genes distal to EXT1. The authors concluded that it probably did not include the TRPS1 gene, which lies proximal to EXT1.

McBrien et al. (2008) reported a boy with a small 8q24.1 microdeletion, characterized by oligo array CGH, that involved EXT1 alone and not TRPS1. He had a mild Langer-Giedion-like phenotype. The authors suggested that this pointed to a functional disturbance of TRPS1. He also had unusual features, including prominent toe pads and fat pads on the soles of his feet, similar to those described in Pierpont syndrome.

Deardorff et al. (2012) reported that children with RAD21 mutations had growth retardation, minor skeletal anomalies, and facial features overlapping those of Cornelia de Lange syndrome. Unlike individuals with NIPBL, SMC1A, or SMC3 mutations, they had much milder cognitive impairment than is seen in classical CdLS.

Deardorff et al. (2012) identified mutations in RAD21, which encodes an integral structural protein of the cohesin complex, in children with a congenital cohesinopathy phenotype. The mutations acted at the interface of RAD21 with the cohesin proteins STAG2 and SMC1A.
Deardorff et al. (2012) found that the RAD21 mutations impaired the cellular DNA damage response and disrupted transcription in a zebrafish model.

Deardorff et al. (2012) suggested that dominant missense mutations in RAD21 cause more severe functional defects than loss-of-function mutations, and lead to worse structural and cognitive clinical findings.

Minor et al. (2014) reported 2 patients with atypical, mild Cornelia de Lange syndrome-like presentation carrying RAD21 mutations. The first patient had developmental delay, hypospadias, inguinal hernia, and dysmorphic features; the second had developmental delay, characteristic facial features, hirsutism, and hand and feet anomalies, with the first patient being milder than the second.

In a patient with mild atypical CdLS, Minor et al. (2014) identified an in-frame intragenic deletion of exon 13 of the RAD21 gene, the first intragenic deletion reported in RAD21. The deletion was inherited from the mother, who had a history of melanoma and other unspecified medical problems; this was described as the first familial case, and the authors discussed variable clinical presentation within families and low penetrance.

In a patient with atypical CdLS including developmental delay, characteristic facial features, hirsutism, and hand and feet anomalies, Minor et al. (2014) identified a c.592_593dup frameshift mutation in the RAD21 gene.

In a patient with mild Cornelia de Lange syndrome, Boyle et al. (2017) identified a novel single-basepair deletion in the RAD21 gene (c.704delG). The deletion was predicted to cause a frameshift resulting in a premature stop codon (p.Ser235IlefsTer19), and the authors predicted it to be deleterious. The deletion was also present in the patient's mother and two aunts.

Boyle et al. (2017) described a family with intrafamilial phenotypic variation associated with a RAD21 deletion. The index patient was classified as having mild Cornelia de Lange syndrome. The patient's mother and two aunts, who also carried the deletion, did not meet the diagnostic criteria for CdLS, and none of them had been suspected of having CdLS or a cohesinopathy before this study.

Boyle et al. (2017) suggested that, based on their study and previous reports, RAD21 variants are associated with incomplete penetrance and that carriers may therefore be underdiagnosed. They noted that RAD21 variants had previously been described in only 5 patients with cohesinopathies.

Gudmundsson et al. (2019) reported a 15-month-old boy with Cornelia de Lange syndrome type 4 who had developmental delay, distinct CdLS-like facial features, gastrointestinal reflux in early infancy, testis retention, prominent digit pads, and diaphragmatic hernia. The authors stated that the patient expanded the clinical description of CdLS4.

In a boy with CdLS4, Gudmundsson et al. (2019) used exome sequencing to identify a de novo heterozygous 3-bp deletion in the RAD21 gene (c.1774_1776del), resulting in an in-frame deletion of glutamine-592 (p.Gln592del). The variant was absent from both healthy parents and was predicted to be disease-causing by bioinformatic analysis. In silico structural modeling predicted that the deletion disrupts contact between RAD21 lys591 and SMC1A residues glu1191 and glu1192, changing the RAD21-SMC1A interface.

Kruszka et al. (2019) reported holoprosencephaly in 4 individuals with variants in the non-X-linked cohesin complex genes SMC3 and RAD21. They also reported holoprosencephaly in 11 individuals with variants in the X-linked cohesin genes STAG2 and SMC1A: 10 had loss-of-function variants and 1 had a missense variant.

Kruszka et al. (2019) concluded that the cohesin complex is an important regulator of median forebrain development. In human neural stem cells, shRNA knockdown of STAG2 and SMC1A caused aberrant expression of the holoprosencephaly-associated genes ZIC2, GLI2, SMAD3, and FGFR1.

Dorval et al. (2020) reported a boy with a mild presentation of Cornelia de Lange syndrome and a molecularly confirmed novel RAD21 mutation. They compared his clinical features with those of previously reported patients who carried other RAD21 intragenic mutations. The authors noted that RAD21 is associated with a milder phenotype and that very few RAD21 intragenic mutations had been identified.

Krab et al. (2020) reported 49 individuals from 33 families with RAD21 alterations: 24 different intragenic sequence variants (2 of them recurrent) and 7 unique microdeletions. Twenty-four of the cases were previously unpublished. Full clinical information was available for 29 patients from 22 families (cohort A). Their phenotype was an attenuated form of CdLS compared with that caused by NIPBL or SMC1A variants, especially for facial morphology, limb anomalies, cognition and behavior. Patients came from Australia, Europe, Turkey, Canada and the United States.

In cohort A (29 patients aged 0 to 61 years; 15 males), Krab et al. (2020) found that all patients had CdLS scores of at least 5. Common features included a short nose (23/26), a long and/or smooth philtrum (26/29), a concave nasal ridge (24/29), thick eyebrows (20/24), long eyelashes (21/26), synophrys (19/28), a short fifth finger (23/28) and postnatal microcephaly (16/28). No patient had a major limb malformation. Small hands (5/27), small feet (3/27), hirsutism (10/26), seizures (2/22) and visual impairment (0/24) were less frequent than in the NIPBL and SMC1A cohorts. Hearing loss occurred in 8 of 24 patients, heart anomalies in 9 of 23, gastroesophageal reflux in 13 of 25 and cleft palate in 6 of 25.

Krab et al. (2020) found that cognition and behavior were attenuated in RAD21 patients compared with NIPBL and SMC1A patients. Of the 29 patients, 16 (55%) had normal cognition or mild intellectual disability, 4 had moderate disability and none had severe or profound disability. All patients aged 3 years or older used some words. Fourteen of 25 had behavioral problems, mainly anxiety, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder features and obsessive-compulsive behavior. Self-injurious behavior and aggression were each seen in only 1 patient.

Krab et al. (2020) summarized the natural history of RAD21-related CdLS. Pregnancy and birth usually progressed normally, and prenatal growth retardation was uncommon. About half of the patients had congenital anomalies such as cleft palate or cardiac anomalies. Diaphragmatic hernia, anal atresia and choanal atresia occurred occasionally. Short stature and microcephaly developed postnatally. Vertebral anomalies (clefts and hemivertebrae) and malformations of structures derived from the embryonic foregut were unusual findings that were relatively frequent in this series.

Krab et al. (2020) noted that the limited clinical information on cohort B suggested that biallelic RAD21 variants can cause Mungan syndrome and that monoallelic variants can cause holoprosencephaly, as in one cohort A case. They also suggested a possible link with schizophrenia but noted that this association may be coincidental. On follow-up, members of the family with Mungan syndrome showed CdLS characteristics that had not been mentioned in the original publication.

In 33 families, Krab et al. (2020) identified 31 different RAD21 alterations: 7 unique deletions (6 of which also included other genes) and 24 intragenic sequence variants. Of the sequence variants, 13 were predicted to be truncating (2 nonsense, 2 splice site and 9 frameshift) and were scattered throughout the gene, whereas missense variants tended to cluster in the functional domains. The variants were frequently familial (9 of 21 index cases in which inheritance could be determined).

Krab et al. (2020) found the recurrent heterozygous RAD21 missense variant c.1753T>C (p.Cys585Arg) in 2 families. It arose de novo in 1 patient and was present in 2 relatives of another family whose parents were not tested. Molecular dynamics modeling predicted that Cys585Arg causes the adjacent Arg586 to lose its salt bridge with Glu577, destabilizing the RAD21-SMC1A domain.

Krab et al. (2020) found the recurrent heterozygous RAD21 nonsense variant c.1756C>T (p.Arg586*) in 2 families. In one of them it was inherited from an affected father. Facial morphology varied between the families carrying this variant.

In a multigenerational family previously reported by Boyle et al. (2017), Krab et al. (2020) updated the data on 5 members who carried the heterozygous RAD21 frameshift variant c.704delG (p.Ser235Ilefs*19). Facial morphology varied within the family.

Krab et al. (2020) reported a patient with a de novo RAD21 in-frame deletion, c.1774_1776del (p.Gln592del), and an unrelated patient with c.1800_1802del (p.Phe600del). Molecular dynamics modeling predicted that Gln592del moves Lys605 and so disturbs the positioning of SMC1A Asn35 at ATPase site 1. Phe600del did not affect RAD21 structure in the model, but the authors considered it likely pathogenic because the patient had classic CdLS and no variants in other known CdLS genes.

Krab et al. (2020) reported a patient with a de novo RAD21 missense variant, c.1808T>C (p.Leu603Pro). Modeling predicted that Pro603 changes the bending angle of the alpha helix and moves Lys605 away from ATPase site 1.

Krab et al. (2020) reported a patient with a de novo RAD21 missense variant in the STAG-binding domain, c.1033T>C (p.Ser345Pro). Modeling predicted that it impairs the RAD21–STAG1/2 interaction by inducing a new curved alpha-helix segment that pulls away from the STAG2 surface. In a previously reported patient, the de novo variant c.1127C>G (p.Pro376Arg) was predicted to form a new salt bridge with STAG2, over-stabilizing the interaction between the two proteins.

Krab et al. (2020) updated the data on the family with Mungan syndrome reported by Bonora et al. (2015), in which 3 affected sibs were homozygous for the RAD21 variant c.1864G>A (p.Ala622Thr). Three further family members were heterozygous and had some clinical features of the CdLS spectrum. However, it remained uncertain whether they had a full CdLS phenotype or whether the variant causes disease in the heterozygous state. Modeling showed no structural change from Ala622Thr, but the authors noted that Ala622 lies next to Thr623, a PLK1 phosphorylation site.

Krab et al. (2020) considered several other modeled or unmodeled RAD21 variants to be likely pathogenic. These were Arg65Gln (c.194G>A), which lies near the Arg-X-Tyr kinase/phosphatase recognition motif around Tyr67; Phe6Val (c.16T>G, de novo), which lies near the phosphorylation site Ser9; and Thr461Ile (c.1382C>T, inherited from the father), which is flanked by serines involved in phosphorylation-regulated release of cohesin from chromosome arms.

Krab et al. (2020) reported a mother and child (family F11) carrying a 665-bp in-frame deletion in RAD21, c.1621-388_1704+193del (p.Asp541_Gln568del), which removes all of exon 13. The child inherited the deletion from the mother.

Krab et al. (2020) identified 7 deletions that included RAD21. Six also removed neighboring genes; one was a 27-kb deletion confined to RAD21 exons 1–9 (8q24.11). Patients with microdeletions tended to have higher CdLS scores and more frequent growth impairment than those with intragenic variants, but the frequency of major malformations and of cognitive and behavioral problems did not differ. Exostoses related to EXT1 haploinsufficiency likely caused upper limb anomalies in some patients with deletions.

Krab et al. (2020) found no difference in CdLS scores or growth parameters between patients with truncating and those with non-truncating RAD21 sequence variants. In 12 of 15 patients with intragenic variants and major malformations or health problems, the variant lay in a protein-binding domain, but the authors noted that it was uncertain whether this was a true association. Variability within and between families was striking, especially for cognition and behavior, and could not be explained by mosaicism in most families.

Krab et al. (2020) suggested that the relatively mild phenotype indicates that RAD21 is not highly intolerant to loss of function, unlike other CdLS genes. They speculated that RAD21 haploinsufficiency may be compensated more effectively than that of other cohesin genes. However, patients with microdeletions or truncating variants did not differ markedly from those with missense variants. Modeling suggested that pathogenic variants in the SMC1A-binding domain disturb the ATPase reaction that is pivotal to opening of the cohesin ring.

Krab et al. (2020) found that applying the CdLS consensus criteria for molecular testing would not have missed any RAD21 variant, and concluded that the CdLS score remains a reliable tool. CdLS was suspected before testing in 13 of 21 index cases. Because familial occurrence was frequent and variability within families was marked, the authors recommended testing parents even when they appear unaffected.
Goel and Parasivam (2020) reported another case of holoprosencephaly associated with a loss-of-function variant in the RAD21 gene.
